claim: In an adult human, 50–70% of the bone marrow cavity is filled with BMAT, which contributes ~10% of the total body fat mass.
source: In an adult human, 50–70% of the bone marrow cavity is filled with BMAT, which contributes ~10% of the total body fat mass (Cawthorn et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cawthorn et al., 2014

claim: BMAT was identified in the 19th century.
source: BMAT was identified in the 19th century, and has been assumed to play significant roles in local bone homeostasis and hematopoiesis (Li et al., 2018; Li and MacDougald, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li and MacDougald, 2021

claim: BMAT has been assumed to play significant roles in local bone homeostasis and hematopoiesis.
source: BMAT was identified in the 19th century, and has been assumed to play significant roles in local bone homeostasis and hematopoiesis (Li et al., 2018; Li and MacDougald, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li and MacDougald, 2021

claim: Clinical associations generally demonstrate inverse relationships between BMAT and bone mass.
source: Clinical associations generally demonstrate inverse relationships between BMAT and bone mass (Shen et al., 2007), or BMAT and circulating immune cells (Polineni et al., 2020), which may be due to the interactions between cells within the bone marrow niche.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2007

claim: Clinical associations generally demonstrate inverse relationships between BMAT and circulating immune cells.
source: Clinical associations generally demonstrate inverse relationships between BMAT and bone mass (Shen et al., 2007), or BMAT and circulating immune cells (Polineni et al., 2020), which may be due to the interactions between cells within the bone marrow niche.
evidence: Supported by citation to Polineni et al., 2020

claim: The bone marrow niche contains osteoblasts, osteoclasts, hematopoietic cells, stromal/mesenchymal cells, blood vessels, and nerves.
source: In addition to bone marrow adipocytes (BMAds), the bone marrow niche contains osteoblasts, osteoclasts, hematopoietic cells, stromal/mesenchymal cells, blood vessels, and nerves (Vogler and Murphy, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogler and Murphy, 1988

claim: Elevated BMAT is inversely correlated with low bone mass of aging and diabetes.
source: For example, elevated BMAT is inversely correlated with low bone mass of aging and diabetes, whereas expansion of BMAT is associated with multiple hematopoietic disorders (Li and MacDougald, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and MacDougald, 2021

claim: Expansion of BMAT is associated with multiple hematopoietic disorders.
source: For example, elevated BMAT is inversely correlated with low bone mass of aging and diabetes, whereas expansion of BMAT is associated with multiple hematopoietic disorders (Li and MacDougald, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and MacDougald, 2021

claim: BMAds potentially influence the marrow niche through cell-to-cell contact, release of extracellular vesicles, and secretion of adipokines and cytokines.
source: In addition to serving as an energy source, BMAds potentially influence the marrow niche through cell-to-cell contact, release of extracellular vesicles, and secretion of adipokines (e.g. adiponectin and leptin) and cytokines (e.g. adipsin, RANK ligand, and stem cell factor; Aaron et al., 2021; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aaron et al., 2021 and Li et al., 2018

claim: Removal of BMAd stimuli in mouse models of lipodystrophy, which lack BMAT, results in increased bone mass.
source: Removal of these stimuli in mouse models of lipodystrophy, which lack BMAT, results in increased bone mass (Corsa et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corsa et al., 2021; Zou et al., 2020; Zou et al., 2019

claim: Use of lipodystrophic models to investigate direct effects of BMAT depletion is confounded by concurrent loss of white and brown adipose depots.
source: However, use of these models to investigate direct effects of BMAT depletion is confounded by concurrent loss of white and brown adipose depots, which also regulate bone mass through myriad mechanisms, including secretion of adipokines (Riddle and Clemens, 2017; Zou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Riddle and Clemens, 2017 and Zou et al., 2019

claim: In rodents, there are two readily identifiable BMAd populations: constitutive BMAT (cBMAT) and regulated BMAT (rBMAT).
source: In rodents, there are two readily identifiable BMAd populations: constitutive BMAT (cBMAT) and regulated BMAT (rBMAT) (Scheller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scheller et al., 2015

claim: cBMAT typically exists in distal tibia and caudal vertebrae, appears early in life, and has the histological appearance of white adipose tissue.
source: cBMAT typically exists in distal tibia and caudal vertebrae, appears early in life, and has the histological appearance of white adipose tissue.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: rBMAT is found in proximal tibia and distal femur, and is comprised of single or clustered BMAds interspersed with hematopoietic cells.
source: rBMAT is found in proximal tibia and distal femur, and is comprised of single or clustered BMAds interspersed with hematopoietic cells.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: cBMAT generally resists change in response to altered physiological states.
source: Although cBMAT generally resists change in response to altered physiological states, rBMAT expands with aging, obesity, diabetes, caloric restriction (CR), irradiation, and estrogen deficiency, and is reduced by cold exposure, β3-agonist, exercise, and vertical sleeve gastrectomy (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2019

claim: rBMAT expands with aging, obesity, diabetes, caloric restriction, irradiation, and estrogen deficiency.
source: Although cBMAT generally resists change in response to altered physiological states, rBMAT expands with aging, obesity, diabetes, caloric restriction (CR), irradiation, and estrogen deficiency, and is reduced by cold exposure, β3-agonist, exercise, and vertical sleeve gastrectomy (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2019

claim: rBMAT is reduced by cold exposure, β3-agonist, exercise, and vertical sleeve gastrectomy.
source: Although cBMAT generally resists change in response to altered physiological states, rBMAT expands with aging, obesity, diabetes, caloric restriction (CR), irradiation, and estrogen deficiency, and is reduced by cold exposure, β3-agonist, exercise, and vertical sleeve gastrectomy (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2019

claim: Steele, 1884 wrote that fat in marrow 'nourishes the skeleton'.
source: Indeed, Steele, 1884 wrote that fat in marrow 'nourishes the skeleton'; however, that conjecture has not been formally tested because current methods to target BMAds lack penetrance or cause recombination in other cell types, such as white adipocytes, osteoblasts, or bone marrow stromal cells, complicating the interpretation of interactions between BMAds and cells of the marrow niche.
evidence: Historical citation to Steele, 1884

claim: Current methods to target BMAds lack penetrance or cause recombination in other cell types, complicating the interpretation of interactions between BMAds and cells of the marrow niche.
source: Indeed, Steele, 1884 wrote that fat in marrow 'nourishes the skeleton'; however, that conjecture has not been formally tested because current methods to target BMAds lack penetrance or cause recombination in other cell types, such as white adipocytes, osteoblasts, or bone marrow stromal cells, complicating the interpretation of interactions between BMAds and cells of the marrow niche.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: The authors created a BMAd-specific Cre mouse model based on expression patterns of endogenous Osterix and Adipoq.
source: To circumvent this problem, we created a BMAd-specific Cre mouse model based on expression patterns of endogenous Osterix and Adipoq, and investigated the role of BMAds as a local energy source by deleting ATGL/Pnpla2, the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental approach in the manuscript

claim: ATGL/Pnpla2 is the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis.
source: To circumvent this problem, we created a BMAd-specific Cre mouse model based on expression patterns of endogenous Osterix and Adipoq, and investigated the role of BMAds as a local energy source by deleting ATGL/Pnpla2, the rate-limiting enzyme of lipolysis.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge stated in the manuscript

claim: BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have impaired BMAd lipolysis.
source: Consistent with Pnpla2 deficiency in white and brown adipocytes (Ahmadian et al., 2011), BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have impaired BMAd lipolysis, resulting in hypertrophy and hyperplasia of BMAT.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Ahmadian et al., 2011

claim: BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have increased size and number of BMAds at baseline.
source: BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have impaired BMAd lipolysis, and increased size and number of BMAds at baseline.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript

claim: Energy from BMAd lipid stores is largely dispensable when mice are fed ad libitum.
source: Although energy from BMAd lipid stores is largely dispensable when mice are fed ad libitum, BMAd lipolysis is necessary to maintain myelopoiesis and bone mass under caloric restriction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no major phenotypes in ad libitum fed mice

claim: BMAd lipolysis is necessary to maintain myelopoiesis and bone mass under caloric restriction.
source: Although energy from BMAd lipid stores is largely dispensable when mice are fed ad libitum, BMAd lipolysis is necessary to maintain myelopoiesis and bone mass under caloric restriction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing phenotypes in caloric restricted mice

claim: BMAd-specific Pnpla2 deficiency compounds the effects of caloric restriction on loss of trabecular bone in male mice.
source: BMAd-specific Pnpla2 deficiency compounds the effects of caloric restriction on loss of trabecular bone in male mice, likely due to impaired osteoblast expression of collagen genes and reduced osteoid synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from μCT and histomorphometry analyses

claim: Reduction of bone mass in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice is likely due to impaired osteoblast expression of collagen genes and reduced osteoid synthesis.
source: BMAd-specific Pnpla2 deficiency compounds the effects of caloric restriction on loss of trabecular bone in male mice, likely due to impaired osteoblast expression of collagen genes and reduced osteoid synthesis.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and histomorphometry showing reduced osteoid

claim: Caloric restriction induces dramatic elevations in extracellular matrix organization and skeletal development genes in bone marrow adipose tissue.
source: RNA sequencing analysis of bone marrow adipose tissue reveals that caloric restriction induces dramatic elevations in extracellular matrix organization and skeletal development genes, and energy from BMAd is required for these adaptations.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data

claim: Energy from BMAd is required for CR-induced adaptations in extracellular matrix organization and skeletal development genes.
source: RNA sequencing analysis of bone marrow adipose tissue reveals that caloric restriction induces dramatic elevations in extracellular matrix organization and skeletal development genes, and energy from BMAd is required for these adaptations.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data showing blunted gene expression in Pnpla2-/- mice

claim: BMAd-derived energy supply is required for bone regeneration upon injury.
source: BMAd-derived energy supply is also required for bone regeneration upon injury, and maintenance of bone mass with cold exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bone defect model

claim: BMAd-derived energy supply is required for maintenance of bone mass with cold exposure.
source: BMAd-derived energy supply is also required for bone regeneration upon injury, and maintenance of bone mass with cold exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cold exposure experiments

claim: Osterix traces to osteoblasts and BMAds, but not to white adipocytes.
source: Based on previous studies showing that Osterix traces to osteoblasts and BMAds, but not to white adipocytes (Chen and Long, 2013; Mizoguchi et al., 2014), we used CRISPR/Cas9 to create Osterix-FLPo mice with an in-frame fusion of Osterix and optimized FLPo, separated by a P2A self-cleaving sequence to allow independent functioning of the two proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Long, 2013 and Mizoguchi et al., 2014

claim: The authors used CRISPR/Cas9 to create Osterix-FLPo mice with an in-frame fusion of Osterix and optimized FLPo, separated by a P2A self-cleaving sequence.
source: Based on previous studies showing that Osterix traces to osteoblasts and BMAds, but not to white adipocytes (Chen and Long, 2013; Mizoguchi et al., 2014), we used CRISPR/Cas9 to create Osterix-FLPo mice with an in-frame fusion of Osterix and optimized FLPo, separated by a P2A self-cleaving sequence to allow independent functioning of the two proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental approach and shown in Figure 1A

claim: EGFP-positive osteocytes, osteoblasts, BMAds, and a subset of marrow stromal cells were observed within the bone of Osterix-FLPo mice bred to FLP-dependent EGFP reporter mice.
source: To validate tissue-specific expression and FLPo efficiency, we bred Osterix-FLPo mice to FLP-dependent EGFP reporter mice, and observed EGFP-positive osteocytes, osteoblasts, BMAds, and a subset of marrow stromal cells within the bone (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: The authors created FLPo-dependent Adipoq-Cre (FAC) mice, which contain an IRES followed by FLPo-dependent Cre in reverse orientation within the 3'-UTR of endogenous Adipoq gene.
source: We next created FLPo-dependent Adipoq-Cre (FAC) mice, which contain an internal ribosome entry sequence (IRES) followed by FLPo-dependent Cre in reverse orientation within the 3'-untranslated region (UTR) of endogenous Adipoq gene (Figure 1D).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental approach and shown in Figure 1D

claim: Adipoq is selectively expressed in adipocytes.
source: However, because Adipoq is selectively expressed in adipocytes (Eguchi et al., 2011), Cre was expressed in BMAds, but not in osteoblasts or other adipose depots.
evidence: Supported by citation to Eguchi et al., 2011

claim: Cre in the correct orientation was only observed in caudal vertebral DNA of mice that were positive for at least one copy each of Osterix and FAC.
source: Consistent with this schema, Cre in the correct orientation (flipped band, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C) was only observed in caudal vertebral DNA of mice that were positive for at least one copy each of Osterix (Mut band) and FAC (Ori band).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: The correct orientation of Cre was observed in mRNA isolated from distal tibiae and caudal vertebrae, but not WAT depots, of Osterix-FLPo mice positive for FAC.
source: The correct orientation of Cre (flipped band) was also observed in mRNA isolated from distal tibiae and caudal vertebrae, but not WAT depots, of Osterix-FLPo mice positive for FAC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Loss of tdTomato and gain of EGFP was observed in BMAT depots of caudal vertebrae and tibiae, but not in brown or white adipose depots, or other tissues/organs in BMAd-Cre mice bred to mT/mG reporter mice.
source: We observed loss of tdTomato and gain of EGFP in BMAT depots of caudal vertebrae (tail) and tibiae, but not in brown or white adipose depots, or other tissues/organs such as liver, pancreas, muscle and spleen (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: The proportion of EGFP-positive BMAds increased with age and number of FAC alleles.
source: To evaluate conditions optimal for Cre-induced recombination, we visualized conversion of tdTomato to EGFP in BMAd-Cre mice at various ages and with different FAC copy numbers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H) and found that the proportion of EGFP-positive BMAds increased with age and number of FAC alleles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H

claim: Cre efficiency was ~80% in both male and female mice over 16 weeks of age with one Cre allele, and over 90% at 12 weeks of age in mice with two Cre alleles.
source: Indeed, Cre efficiency was ~80% in both male and female mice over 16 weeks of age with one Cre allele, and over 90% at 12 weeks of age in mice with two Cre alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I

claim: A randomly inserted Adipoq-Cre bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) causes recombination in osteoblasts.
source: Previous studies found that a randomly inserted Adipoq-Cre bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) causes recombination in osteoblasts (Bozec et al., 2013; Eguchi et al., 2011; Mukohira et al., 2019); thus, we tested whether this observation is true in BMAd-Cre mice, which rely on endogenous Adipoq expression that is further restricted by Osterix.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bozec et al., 2013; Eguchi et al., 2011; Mukohira et al., 2019

claim: Only tdTomato-positive cells were detectable on trabecular bone surfaces in BMAd-Cre mice bred to mT/mG reporter mice, suggesting that osteoblasts were not targeted.
source: When BMAd-Cre mice were bred to mT/mG reporter mice, only tdTomato-positive cells were detectable on trabecular bone surfaces (Figure 1F), suggesting that osteoblasts were not targeted.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Labeling of a small subset of stromal/dendritic cells was consistently observed in BMAd-Cre mice, likely due to expression of Adipoq within this cell population.
source: However, labeling of a small subset of stromal/dendritic cells was consistently observed, likely due to expression of Adipoq within this cell population (Mukohira et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and citation to Mukohira et al., 2019

claim: Insertion of the IRES-Cre cassette caused a small, non-significant decrease in Adipoq mRNA expression in whole caudal vertebrae or distal tibiae.
source: We found that insertion of the IRES-Cre cassette caused a small, non-significant decrease in Adipoq mRNA expression in whole caudal vertebrae or distal tibiae, whereas adiponectin mRNA in white adipose tissue was elevated by more than threefold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Adiponectin mRNA in white adipose tissue was elevated by more than threefold in FAC mice.
source: We found that insertion of the IRES-Cre cassette caused a small, non-significant decrease in Adipoq mRNA expression in whole caudal vertebrae or distal tibiae, whereas adiponectin mRNA in white adipose tissue was elevated by more than threefold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Expression of adiponectin protein in WAT and BMAT was decreased by ~50% in FAC mice.
source: Instead, it appeared that the 2 kb IRES-Cre cassette within the 3'-UTR impairs translatability of the mRNA since expression of adiponectin protein in WAT and BMAT was decreased by ~50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C

claim: Circulating adiponectin concentrations were decreased in FAC mice.
source: Circulating adiponectin concentrations were decreased even further (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), suggesting that flux of translated adiponectin protein was impaired through the secretion pathway.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F

claim: Hypoadiponectinemia is associated with insulin resistance.
source: Of note, hypoadiponectinemia is associated with insulin resistance (Cook and Semple, 2010; Li et al., 2021), with discrepant effects reported on osteogenesis (Lewis et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook and Semple, 2010 and Li et al., 2021

claim: Body weight, glucose tolerance, WAT depot weights, and tibial trabecular and cortical bone variables were unaffected by hypoadiponectinemia in BMAd-Cre mice.
source: Thus, we evaluated systemic metabolism in BMAd-Cre mice and found that body weight, glucose tolerance, WAT depot weights, and tibial trabecular and cortical bone variables were unaffected by this degree of hypoadiponectinemia (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–P).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–P

claim: Mutant Pnpla2 mRNA was observed in caudal vertebrae of BMAd-Pnpla2 mice, but not in WAT.
source: We validated the deletion of ATGL in caudal vertebrae, because cBMAT is abundant in this location. Mutant Pnpla2 mRNA was observed in caudal vertebrae of BMAd-Pnpla2 mice, but not in WAT (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Immunofluorescent staining confirmed loss of ATGL in proximal tibial rBMAds of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: Immunofluorescent staining confirmed loss of ATGL in proximal tibial rBMAds of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: ATGL protein was reduced substantially in caudal vertebrae, but not in subcutaneous WAT of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: ATGL protein was reduced substantially in caudal vertebrae, but not in subcutaneous WAT (Figure 2C), which further confirmed specificity of BMAd-Cre recombinase for BMAT.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: BMAT volume was significantly increased in proximal tibiae and throughout the endocortical compartment of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: We found that BMAT volume was significantly increased in proximal tibiae and throughout the endocortical compartment of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, whereas differences in BMAT volume were not observed in distal tibiae, which was almost completely occupied by BMAT in control mice (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F

claim: Differences in BMAT volume were not observed in distal tibiae of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, which was almost completely occupied by BMAT in control mice.
source: We found that BMAT volume was significantly increased in proximal tibiae and throughout the endocortical compartment of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, whereas differences in BMAT volume were not observed in distal tibiae, which was almost completely occupied by BMAT in control mice (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D–F

claim: Histological analyses revealed increased BMAd number in proximal tibiae of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: Histological analyses revealed increased BMAd number in proximal tibiae of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Depletion of Pnpla2 caused BMAd hypertrophy in both proximal and distal tibia.
source: Depletion of Pnpla2 also caused BMAd hypertrophy in both proximal and distal tibia, with an increased proportion of BMAds larger than 500 μm2 observed in proximal tibia, and larger than 1000 μm2 observed in distal tibia (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I and J

claim: Secretion of basal glycerol and NEFA from ex vivo cultured explants of distal tibial BMAT was not different between genotypes.
source: Secretion of basal glycerol and NEFA from ex vivo cultured explants of distal tibial BMAT was not different between genotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from ex vivo lipolysis assay

claim: Forskolin treatment greatly increased lipolysis in BMAT explants from control mice, but secretion of glycerol and NEFA from BMAd-Pnpla2-/- explants remained unchanged from basal rates.
source: On the other hand, forskolin treatment greatly increased lipolysis in BMAT explants from control mice, but secretion of glycerol and NEFA from BMAd-Pnpla2-/- explants remained unchanged from basal rates (Figure 2K–M).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K–M

claim: BMAds of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have impaired lipolysis.
source: These results confirm that BMAds of BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice have impaired lipolysis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from ex vivo lipolysis assay data

claim: In mice fed normal chow ad libitum, no differences were observed in body weight, glucose tolerance, or weights of soft tissue between BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice and controls.
source: In mice fed normal chow ad libitum, we did not observe differences in body weight, glucose tolerance, or weights of soft tissue, including subcutaneous WAT (sWAT), epididymal WAT (eWAT), and liver (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E), which further confirmed the tissue-specificity of our BMAd-Pnpla2 knockout model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-E

claim: Pnpla2 deficiency caused expansion of proximal tibial rBMAT in ad libitum fed mice.
source: As observed above, Pnpla2 deficiency caused expansion of proximal tibial rBMAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: When dietary energy was readily available, trabecular bone volume fraction, bone mineral density and trabecular number tended to be lower in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, but statistical differences were not observed.
source: Interestingly, when dietary energy was readily available, trabecular bone volume fraction, bone mineral density and trabecular number tended to be lower in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, but statistical differences were not observed (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–C

claim: BMAd-Pnpla2-/- male mice fed CR diet had reduced trabecular bone volume fraction, connective density, and bone mineral density when compared to controls.
source: Despite having a similar amount of rBMAT, BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed CR diet had reduced trabecular bone volume fraction, connective density, and bone mineral density when compared to controls (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: The reduction in bone mass in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice is due to decreased trabecular bone number and increased trabecular spacing, without effects on trabecular thickness.
source: This reduction in bone mass is due to decreased trabecular bone number and increased trabecular spacing, without effects on trabecular thickness (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: BMAds are a source of NEFA for vicinal osteoblasts.
source: BMAds are a source of NEFA for vicinal osteoblasts (Maridas et al., 2019); thus, the reduction in trabecular bone in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice likely resulted from impaired osteoblast function due to insufficient energy available in the bone marrow niche.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maridas et al., 2019

claim: The reduction in trabecular bone in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice likely resulted from impaired osteoblast function due to insufficient energy available in the bone marrow niche.
source: BMAds are a source of NEFA for vicinal osteoblasts (Maridas et al., 2019); thus, the reduction in trabecular bone in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice likely resulted from impaired osteoblast function due to insufficient energy available in the bone marrow niche.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and established knowledge

claim: A trend towards reduced NEFA concentrations in bone marrow supernatant of CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice was observed.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed a trend (p=0.07) towards reduced NEFA concentrations in bone marrow supernatant of CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, whilst circulating glycerol and NEFA concentrations were not different between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1T and U).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1T and U

claim: Circulating glycerol and NEFA concentrations were not different between genotypes in CR mice.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed a trend (p=0.07) towards reduced NEFA concentrations in bone marrow supernatant of CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, whilst circulating glycerol and NEFA concentrations were not different between genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1T and U).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1T and U

claim: Comparable adiponectin concentrations between BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ and BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice excludes the possibility that differences in circulating adiponectin may confound the bone phenotype in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: Although FAC mice have hypoadiponectinemia at baseline, circulating adiponectin was still increased dramatically in response to CR. Comparable adiponectin concentrations between BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ and BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1V) excludes the possibility that differences in circulating adiponectin may confound the bone phenotype in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1V

claim: Changes in cortical bone area and thickness were not observed in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice with either ad libitum or CR diet.
source: Finally, changes in cortical bone area and thickness were not observed in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice with either ad libitum or CR diet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D), perhaps because cortical bone surfaces are less active.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D

claim: Osteoblast and osteoclast numbers and osteoclast surface were not changed by BMAd-Pnpla2 deficiency under ad libitum conditions.
source: Osteoblast and osteoclast numbers and osteoclast surface were not changed by BMAd-Pnpla2 deficiency under ad libitum conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F

claim: Markers for bone resorption (CTX-1) and osteoclast activation (TRACP5b) were decreased or showed a strong trend towards reduction in ad libitum fed BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: Although circulating markers of bone formation (P1NP) and osteoclast activation (RANK Ligand) were not altered in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, markers for bone resorption (CTX-1) and osteoclast activation (TRACP5b) were decreased or showed a strong trend towards reduction, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G-J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G-J

claim: Osteoblast numbers were not altered by a deficiency of BMAT lipolysis with CR.
source: Although with CR, osteoblast numbers were not altered by a deficiency of BMAT lipolysis, the bone formation marker P1NP was decreased (Figure 3G and I), suggesting that osteoblast functions were impaired.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and I

claim: The bone formation marker P1NP was decreased in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, suggesting that osteoblast functions were impaired.
source: Although with CR, osteoblast numbers were not altered by a deficiency of BMAT lipolysis, the bone formation marker P1NP was decreased (Figure 3G and I), suggesting that osteoblast functions were impaired.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and I

claim: Osteoclast numbers were increased in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, but the osteoclast surface per bone surface was not changed and the osteoclast activation marker, TRACP5b, was decreased.
source: Osteoclast numbers were increased in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, but the osteoclast surface per bone surface (Oc.S/BS) was not changed and the osteoclast activation marker, TRACP5b, was decreased (Figure 3H and J), suggesting osteoclast function was inhibited.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H and J

claim: A trend towards thinner osteoid layers without affecting osteoid surface was observed in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: We then visualized and quantified osteoid thickness with Goldner's trichrome staining and observed a trend towards thinner osteoid layers without affecting osteoid surface (Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2M), which could be secondary to impaired secretion of collagen matrix by osteoblasts or to enhanced bone mineralization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 2M

claim: BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice had less bone-forming surface, as indicated by reduced single-labelled surface (sLS) and mineral surface (MS).
source: Further, we injected mice with calcein to label those bone surfaces undergoing active mineralization. Dynamic histomorphometry data suggests that BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice had less bone-forming surface, as indicated by reduced single-labelled surface (sLS) and mineral surface (MS) (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L

claim: There were no differences in double-labelled bone surface, inter-label width, mineral apposition rate or osteoid maturation time in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: There were no differences in double-labelled bone surface, inter-label width, mineral apposition rate or osteoid maturation time (Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2N), suggesting that bone mineralization is not affected by loss of BMAd lipolysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2N

claim: Bone mineralization is not affected by loss of BMAd lipolysis.
source: There were no differences in double-labelled bone surface, inter-label width, mineral apposition rate or osteoid maturation time (Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2N), suggesting that bone mineralization is not affected by loss of BMAd lipolysis.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2N

claim: BMAd Pnpla2 deletion did not cause changes in trabecular or cortical bone variables in female mice under CR.
source: Whereas CR increased trabecular bone BV/TV, and decreased Tb. Sp, BMAd Pnpla2 deletion did not cause changes in trabecular or cortical bone variables in female mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E

claim: Complete blood cell analyses did not reveal substantial differences in white or red blood cell populations influenced by diet or genotype in female mice.
source: In addition, complete blood cell analyses did not reveal substantial differences in white or red blood cell populations influenced by diet or genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F

claim: OVX-associated trabecular bone loss was partially eliminated by CR treatment.
source: Interestingly, despite the dramatic increases of BMAT with CR or BMAd-Pnpla2 deficiency, OVX-associated trabecular bone loss was partially eliminated by CR treatment, which was evidenced by a relative increase in bone volume fraction (Tb. BV/TV) and trabecular number (Tb. N) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E and F

claim: The metabolic benefits of CR diet may combat detrimental effects of estrogen deficiency and/or aging.
source: These data suggest that the metabolic benefits of CR diet may combat detrimental effects of estrogen deficiency and/or aging.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from OVX+CR experiments

claim: With OVX, the loss of BMAd ATGL caused a slight reduction in trabecular bone mineral density and thickness compared to OVX controls.
source: Although not observed in intact mice, with OVX Pnpla2-deficient mice, the loss of BMAd ATGL caused a slight reduction in trabecular bone mineral density (Tb. BMD) and thickness (Tb. Th) compared to OVX controls (revealed by two-way ANOVA analysis) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4F

claim: A single rBMAd connects to almost 100 hematopoietic cells.
source: A single rBMAd connects to almost 100 hematopoietic cells (Robles et al., 2019), suggesting that BMAds potentially serve as important local energy sources for hematopoiesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Robles et al., 2019

claim: When fed ad libitum, male BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice did not exhibit differences in mature blood cells populations or in bone marrow hematopoietic cell populations.
source: However, when fed ad libitum, male BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice did not exhibit differences in mature blood cells populations, as assessed by complete blood cell counts (Supplementary file 1) or in bone marrow hematopoietic cell populations, as assessed by flow cytometry (Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary files 1 and 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: A reduced percentage of bone marrow mature neutrophils was observed in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: However, we did observe a reduced percentage of bone marrow mature neutrophils in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2), perhaps due to impaired maturation of granulocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Supplementary files 1 and 2

claim: Significant interactions between genotype and time were observed for neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils following irradiation, suggesting BMAd-Pnpla2 deficiency specifically influenced myeloid lineage cells.
source: During the recovery phase, three-way ANOVA analyses revealed that differences in time (days) and diet (AL vs CR) were observed for total white blood cells, lymphocytes, and red blood cells, while significant interactions between genotype (BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ vs BMAd-Pnpla2-/-) and time were observed for neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils, suggesting BMAd-Pnpla2 deficiency specifically influenced myeloid lineage cells.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: HSPCs and mature/immature hematopoietic cells were not influenced by deficiency of BMAd-lipolysis in ad libitum fed mice nine days after irradiation.
source: Nine days after irradiation, HSPCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G) and mature/immature hematopoietic cells (Figure 4A–H) were not influenced by deficiency of BMAd-lipolysis in ad libitum fed mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G and Figure 4A–H

claim: CR decreased bone marrow cellularity and most HSPC populations in control mice.
source: However, CR decreased bone marrow cellularity (BMNC) (Figure 4A), and most HSPC populations in control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: The recovery of neutrophils, preneutrophils, immature and mature neutrophils following irradiation was impaired by CR, and Pnpla2-deficiency further reduced ability of neutrophils and mature neutrophils to regenerate.
source: The recovery of neutrophils, preneutrophils, immature and mature neutrophils following irradiation was impaired by CR, and Pnpla2-deficiency further reduced ability of neutrophils and mature neutrophils to regenerate (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E–H

claim: The proliferative capacity of macrophage progenitors (CFU-M) was impaired when derived from BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed ad libitum, or when derived from CR mice of either genotype.
source: The proliferative capacity of macrophage progenitors (CFU-M) was impaired when derived from BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed ad libitum, or when derived from CR mice of either genotype (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J

claim: CR marrow produced fewer granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (CFU-GM), which was further reduced when isolated from mice with impaired BMAd-lipolysis.
source: CR marrow produced fewer granulocyte-macrophage progenitors (CFU-GM), which was further reduced when isolated from mice with impaired BMAd-lipolysis (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4K

claim: Proliferative and differentiation capacities of cultured myeloid cell progenitors may have been reprogrammed in the marrow niche when their energy supply was limited either by CR or impaired BMAd lipolysis.
source: These data suggest that proliferative and differentiation capacities of cultured myeloid cell progenitors may have been reprogrammed in the marrow niche when their energy supply was limited either by CR or impaired BMAd lipolysis (Figure 4L).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 4L

claim: CR changed expression of 1026 genes compared to ad libitum controls in bone marrow plugs from distal tibiae.
source: By our criteria (padj <0.05, |log2 fold change|>1), CR changed expression of 1026 genes compared to ad libitum controls (left).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data

claim: Pnpla2 deficiency alone only altered 10 genes in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed ad libitum.
source: Although Pnpla2 deficiency alone only altered 10 genes in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed ad libitum (middle), loss of Pnpla2 in CR mice caused alterations in 1060 genes (right) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Loss of Pnpla2 in CR mice caused alterations in 1060 genes.
source: Although Pnpla2 deficiency alone only altered 10 genes in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice fed ad libitum (middle), loss of Pnpla2 in CR mice caused alterations in 1060 genes (right) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Approximately 80% of genes fell in cluster 1, which contained genes upregulated by CR in control mice, with induction largely blocked by Pnpla2 deficiency in CR mice.
source: Approximately 80% of genes fell in cluster 1, which contained genes upregulated by CR in control mice, with induction largely blocked by Pnpla2 deficiency in CR mice.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data analysis

claim: Genes in cluster 1 were associated with vasculature development and cellular response to growth factor stimulus.
source: Pathway analyses of cluster 1 with Metascape (https://metascape.org) revealed that regulated genes were associated with vasculature development and cellular response to growth factor stimulus, which likely reflects adaptation mechanisms to compensate for energy insufficiency (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Genes associated with skeletal system development, extracellular matrix organization, and adipogenesis pathways were upregulated by CR in control mice, but these effects were blunted by Pnpla2 deletion.
source: In addition, genes associated with skeletal system development, extracellular matrix organization, and adipogenesis pathways were upregulated by CR in control mice, but these effects were blunted by Pnpla2 deletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Upregulation of two monocarboxylate transporters, Slc16a11 and Slc16a4, suggests a potential mechanism for fueling cellular metabolism in cluster 2 genes.
source: Cluster 2 includes genes that were mildly upregulated by CR in control mice and were further increased with Pnpla2-deficiency. Although no specific pathways were enriched in this gene set, upregulation of two monocarboxylate transporters, Slc16a11 and Slc16a4, suggests a potential mechanism for fueling cellular metabolism, and perhaps for the energy source underlying expansion of BMAd with CR and BMAd Pnpla2 deletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Cluster 3 genes were associated with B cell proliferation and interleukin-8 production.
source: Cluster 3 highlighted genes that were downregulated by CR treatment regardless of genotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), and that were associated with B cell proliferation and interleukin-8 production, which may partially explain changes in hematopoietic cellularity.
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: Cluster 4 contained 80 genes that were down-regulated independently by CR and Pnpla2-deficiency, and were associated with regulation of ossification and calcium-mediated signaling.
source: Cluster 4 contained 80 genes that were down-regulated independently by CR and Pnpla2-deficiency, and were associated with regulation of ossification and calcium-mediated signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F

claim: 66% of genes regulated by CR in control mice did not meet criteria for regulated expression by CR in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: To evaluate further whether BMAd-Pnpla2 is required for the adaptation of BMAT to CR, we graphically ordered genes from those maximally induced to those most repressed by CR in control mice (Figure 5B; red dots). Of these genes, 66% did not meet our criteria for regulated expression by CR in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (blue dots).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Adipogenic genes, including Adipoq, Fabp4, Cebpa, Lipe, Lpl, Ppara, Pparg, Scd1, Plin1, Cd36, Fasn, and Acaca, were upregulated by CR in control mice.
source: A heatmap showed that the adipogenic genes, including Adipoq, Fabp4, Cebpa, Lipe, Lpl, Ppara, Pparg, Scd1, Plin1, Cd36, Fasn, and Acaca, were upregulated by CR in control mice (Figure 5D), a subset of which were confirmed by qPCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5D and qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B

claim: Whereas CR BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ and BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice had comparable amounts of BMAT, adipocyte gene expression was greatly suppressed in mice with BMAT lacking Pnpla2.
source: It is important to note that whereas CR BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ and BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice had comparable amounts of BMAT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1O and P), adipocyte gene expression was greatly suppressed in mice with BMAT lacking Pnpla2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1O and P and Figure 5D

claim: Adipocyte-specific deletion of Pnpla2 results in decreased expression of genes associated with lipid uptake, synthesis, and adipogenesis.
source: This observation is consistent with prior work showing that adipocyte-specific deletion of Pnpla2 results in decreased expression of genes associated with lipid uptake, synthesis, and adipogenesis (Schoiswohl et al., 2015), perhaps because NEFA and associated metabolites act as PPAR ligands (Mottillo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schoiswohl et al., 2015 and Mottillo et al., 2012

claim: Genes related to endogenous fatty acid biosynthesis were increased by CR in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice, but not in mice lacking Pnpla2.
source: In addition, genes related to endogenous fatty acid biosynthesis were also increased by CR in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice, but not in mice lacking Pnpla2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C

claim: Myeloid leukocyte differentiation genes were increased by CR in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice, but not in mice lacking Pnpla2.
source: Interestingly, myeloid leukocyte differentiation genes followed a similar pattern (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), which may contribute to the reduced neutrophil production and impaired myeloid cell proliferation of CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2, and Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D

claim: Osteoblast-derived alkaline phosphatase (Alpl), Col1a1 and Col1a2, and bone marrow Fgf/Fgfr and Wnt signaling-related molecules were highly induced by CR in control mice but not in Pnpla2-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, osteoblast-derived alkaline phosphatase (Alpl), Col1a1 and Col1a2, and bone marrow Fgf/Fgfr and Wnt signaling-related molecules were highly induced by CR in control mice but not in Pnpla2-deficient mice (Figure 5E); many of these genes are also found in the ossification pathway.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Multiple collagen genes, Lox, and Adamts family members were upregulated by CR in control mice, with effects largely eliminated by Pnpla2 deficiency.
source: Multiple collagen genes, Lox, and Adamts (A Disintegrin and Metalloproteinase with Thrombospondin motifs) family members, which are multidomain extracellular protease enzymes and play key roles in extracellular matrix remodeling, were also upregulated by CR in control mice, with effects largely eliminated by Pnpla2 deficiency (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5F

claim: 20 collagen genes were significantly up-regulated in control mice following CR, whereas only four collagen genes were elevated in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: In this regard, 20 collagen genes were significantly up-regulated in control mice following CR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E), whereas only four collagen genes were elevated in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E

claim: Under conditions of limited dietary energy, BMAds provide energy to maintain osteoblast functions, including the secretion of collagen matrix for osteoid synthesis.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that under conditions of limited dietary energy, BMAds provide energy to maintain osteoblast functions, including the secretion of collagen matrix for osteoid synthesis.
evidence: Inference based on RNA sequencing and histomorphometry data

claim: CR impaired formation of bone in the trabecular (endocortical) region of interest, resulting in decreased bone volume fraction, mineral density, and mineral content.
source: As expected, CR impaired formation of bone in the trabecular (endocortical) region of interest (ROI), resulting in decreased bone volume fraction, mineral density, and mineral content (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Effects of CR on impaired bone regeneration were mimicked by BMAd-specific Pnpla2 deletion.
source: Importantly, these effects of CR were mimicked by BMAd-specific Pnpla2 deletion; however, gene deletion did not compound effects of CR on impaired bone regeneration, perhaps because newly-formed bone volume was already low with either CR or Pnpla2 deficiency alone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bone regeneration experiments

claim: Both bone marrow stromal and periosteal cells contribute to the cortical bone regeneration and are derived from common mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Of note, both bone marrow stromal and periosteal cells contribute to the cortical bone regeneration and are derived from common mesenchymal progenitors (Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duchamp de Lageneste et al., 2018

claim: CR impaired formation of new woven bone in the cortical compartment by decreasing bone volume fraction, mineral density, and mineral content.
source: CR also impaired formation of new woven bone in the cortical compartment by decreasing bone volume fraction, mineral density, and mineral content.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bone regeneration experiments

claim: Effects of CR on the cortical compartment are mimicked by BMAd-specific depletion of Pnpla2.
source: As with bone formation in the trabecular compartment, effects of CR on the cortical compartment are mimicked by BMAd-specific depletion of Pnpla2, and effects of impaired BMAd lipolysis did not exacerbate CR-induced impaired bone regeneration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Under conditions where energy requirements are high, BMAd provide a critical local energy source for early-stage bone regeneration.
source: Taken together, these data provide compelling evidence that under conditions where energy requirements are high, BMAd provide a critical local energy source for early-stage bone regeneration.
evidence: Inference based on bone regeneration experimental data

claim: Cold exposure resulted in smaller rBMAds within the proximal tibia of BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice.
source: As expected (Scheller et al., 2015; Scheller et al., 2019), cold exposure resulted in smaller rBMAds within the proximal tibia of BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F and citations to Scheller et al., 2015 and Scheller et al., 2019

claim: rBMAd size was increased at baseline in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, with no reduction observed with cold exposure.
source: In contrast, rBMAd size was increased at baseline in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, with no reduction observed with cold exposure (Figure 6E and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and G

claim: Intact BMAd lipolysis was required for reduction of BMAd size with cold exposure.
source: These data indicate that intact BMAd lipolysis was required for reduction of BMAd size with cold exposure.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from cold exposure experiments

claim: Trabecular bone of the proximal tibia was maintained in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice with cold stress, but trabecular bone volume fraction declined with cold exposure in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: We then evaluated bone mass by μCT and found that whereas trabecular bone of the proximal tibia was maintained in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice with cold stress, trabecular bone volume fraction declined with cold exposure in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice and bone mineral density showed a similar trend (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Lipolysis from vicinal BMAds is important for maintenance of bone when energy needs are high or when energy supply is limited.
source: These results suggest that lipolysis from vicinal BMAds is important for maintenance of bone when energy needs are high or when energy supply is limited.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from cold exposure experiments

claim: The bone formation marker, P1NP, decreased in cold-exposed BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice compared to room temperature controls, suggesting that osteoblast functions were impaired.
source: However, the bone formation marker, P1NP, decreased in cold-exposed BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice compared to room temperature controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that osteoblast functions were impaired.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: Control BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ male mice were more vulnerable to cold-induced bone loss than female mice.
source: Interestingly, control BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ male mice were more vulnerable to cold-induced bone loss than female mice, with significant reductions of trabecular bone volume fraction, mineral density, and thickness.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from cold exposure experiments in male and female mice

claim: Cold exposure decreased trabecular connective density and trabecular number, and increased trabecular bone spacing in male BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice.
source: Although cold stimuli did not affect the microstructure parameters of trabecular bone in BMAd-Pnpla2+/+ mice, cold exposure decreased trabecular connective density and trabecular number, and increased trabecular bone spacing in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G,I,J and ).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G,I,J

claim: There is sexual dimorphism in the response of bone to cold.
source: Taken together, these data highlight sexual dimorphism in the response of bone to cold, and that in both males and females, a further loss of bone is observed when BMAT lipolysis is impaired.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from cold exposure experiments in male and female mice

claim: In both males and females, a further loss of bone is observed when BMAT lipolysis is impaired under cold exposure.
source: Taken together, these data highlight sexual dimorphism in the response of bone to cold, and that in both males and females, a further loss of bone is observed when BMAT lipolysis is impaired.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from cold exposure experiments

claim: The authors developed and tested for the first time, a BMAd-specific mouse model to understand the function of bone marrow adipose tissue during times of nutritional, hormonal, mechanical and environmental stress.
source: In the current study, we developed and tested for the first time, a BMAd-specific mouse model to more clearly understand the function of bone marrow adipose tissue, particularly during times of nutritional, hormonal, mechanical and environmental stress.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: Expansion of BMAT is not sufficient to cause bone loss.
source: Surprisingly, despite expansion of BMAT in ad libitum-fed BMAd-Pnpla2-/- male and female mice, we did not observe differences in skeletal parameters, indicating that expansion of BMAT is not sufficient to cause bone loss, and that the correlation between elevated fracture risk and expansion of BMAT under a variety of clinical situations is not necessarily a causal relationship.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing no bone phenotype with BMAT expansion in ad libitum fed mice

claim: The correlation between elevated fracture risk and expansion of BMAT under a variety of clinical situations is not necessarily a causal relationship.
source: Surprisingly, despite expansion of BMAT in ad libitum-fed BMAd-Pnpla2-/- male and female mice, we did not observe differences in skeletal parameters, indicating that expansion of BMAT is not sufficient to cause bone loss, and that the correlation between elevated fracture risk and expansion of BMAT under a variety of clinical situations is not necessarily a causal relationship.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: The critical role of BMAd lipolysis in fueling osteoblasts was observed in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- male mice only when energy needs were high, or when the availability of dietary energy was low.
source: The critical role of BMAd lipolysis in fueling osteoblasts was observed in BMAd-Pnpla2-/- male mice only when energy needs were high, or when the availability of dietary energy was low.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data from CR, bone regeneration, and cold exposure experiments

claim: Cellular protein synthesis typically uses 25–30% of the oxygen consumption coupled to ATP synthesis.
source: Of note, cellular protein synthesis typically uses 25–30% of the oxygen consumption coupled to ATP synthesis (Rolfe and Brown, 1997), and this percentage may be higher in osteoblasts since protein synthesis and translation are integral to osteoblast function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rolfe and Brown, 1997

claim: Fatty acids contribute substantially to the energy demands of bone tissue and cells.
source: Additionally, fatty acids contribute substantially to the energy demands of bone tissue and cells (Adamek et al., 1987), and in the absence of BMAd lipolysis, these energy needs must be met from circulating lipids, glucose, lactate, and amino acids.
evidence: Supported by citation to Adamek et al., 1987

claim: Uptake of fatty acids by osteoblasts is likely mediated by the CD36 fatty acid translocase, which is required in mice to maintain osteoblast numbers and activity.
source: Uptake of fatty acids by osteoblasts is likely mediated by the CD36 fatty acid translocase, which is required in mice to maintain osteoblast numbers and activity (Kevorkova et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kevorkova et al., 2013

claim: Impairment of fatty acid oxidation in osteoblasts and osteocytes led to reduced postnatal bone acquisition in female, but not male mice.
source: Further, impairment of fatty acid oxidation in osteoblasts and osteocytes led to reduced postnatal bone acquisition in female, but not male mice.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript

claim: Significant increases in the osteoid thickness, osteoid volume per bone volume, and the osteoid maturation time suggest that a mineralization defect occurs in mice unable to oxidize fatty acids obtained from BMAds and circulation.
source: Interestingly, significant increases in the osteoid thickness, osteoid volume per bone volume, and the osteoid maturation time suggest that a mineralization defect occurs in mice unable to oxidize fatty acids obtained not only from BMAds, but also from circulation (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017

claim: ATGL deficiency prevents cAMP-dependent degradation of TXNIP and thus reduces glucose uptake and lactate secretion.
source: For example, ATGL deficiency prevents cAMP-dependent degradation of TXNIP and thus reduces glucose uptake and lactate secretion (Beg et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beg et al., 2021

claim: ATGL-catalyzed lipolysis provides essential mediators to increase activity of PGC-1α/PPARα and PPARδ pathways.
source: ATGL-catalyzed lipolysis also provides essential mediators to increase activity of PGC-1α/PPARα and PPARδpathways (Haemmerle et al., 2011; Khan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haemmerle et al., 2011 and Khan et al., 2015

claim: It is conceivable that ATGL deficiency may alter the BMAd transcriptome and secretome to influence the marrow niche independent of its role as a fuel source.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that ATGL deficiency may alter the BMAd transcriptome and secretome to influence the marrow niche independent of its role as a fuel source.
evidence: Speculation based on known functions of ATGL

claim: Skeletal sites containing low BMAd numbers, including vertebrae, sternum, ribs and pelvis, may allow compensatory formation of circulating mature blood cells.
source: One possibility is that skeletal sites containing low BMAd numbers, including vertebrae, sternum, ribs and pelvis, may allow compensatory formation of circulating mature blood cells (Kricun, 1985).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to Kricun, 1985

claim: Glucose serves as the major source of energy for glycolysis and oxidative metabolism in hematopoietic progenitors and mature cells.
source: Although hematopoietic progenitors and mature cells can use lipids for energy, glucose serves as the major source of energy for glycolysis and oxidative metabolism in these cell populations (Jeon et al., 2020; Roy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jeon et al., 2020 and Roy et al., 2018

claim: There is a great deal of metabolic flexibility when it comes to fuel sources for hematopoiesis.
source: It is perhaps unsurprising, given the importance of blood cell production in maintaining life, that there is a great deal of metabolic flexibility when it comes to fuel sources for hematopoiesis.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and established knowledge

claim: Fatty acid oxidation is required for HSC asymmetric division to retain the stem cell properties.
source: We did not profile the metabolic changes of HSPCs in CR BMAd-Pnpla2-/- mice, but it has been reported that fatty acid oxidation is required for HSC asymmetric division to retain the stem cell properties (Ito et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 2012

claim: BMAds are a local energy source that support myeloid cell lineage regeneration following irradiation, and maintain progenitor differentiation capacity when systemic energy is limiting.
source: In summary, we have developed a novel mouse model to specifically evaluate the importance of BMAds in adult life and during times of nutritional, hormonal, environmental and mechanical stress. We report that BMAds are a local energy source that support myeloid cell lineage regeneration following irradiation, and maintain progenitor differentiation capacity when systemic energy is limiting.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: BMAT serves a highly specialized function to maintain bone mass and osteoblast function in times of elevated local energy needs such as with bone regeneration, increased whole body energy needs from cold exposure, or when dietary energy is limited due to CR.
source: In addition, we find that BMAT serves a highly specialized function to maintain bone mass and osteoblast function in times of elevated local energy needs such as with bone regeneration, increased whole body energy needs from cold exposure, or when dietary energy is limited due to CR.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Steele's instincts in 1884 when he wrote that fat from marrow 'nourishes the skeleton' are largely borne out by modern experimentation.
source: Thus, Steele's instincts in 1884 when he wrote that fat from marrow 'nourishes the skeleton' are largely borne out by modern experimentation.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental findings
